newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Berlin sells BEWAG because of financial woes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Berlin sells BEWAG because of financial woes.

text.p: Struggling under a mountain of debt, Berlin said on Tuesday it was reluctantly selling one of its most attractive assets in a bid to avoid bankruptcy.

But the 3.19 billion marks ($1.9 billion) Berlin will collect from the sale of Berliner Kraft und Licht AG (BEWAG) only partially helps to plug gaping holes with a deficit projected to hit 5.45 billion marks in its 45-billion mark 1997 budget.

"BEWAG is being sold primarily because the city is bankrupt or nearly bankrupt because the federal government has left us standing in the rain," said Berlin's Senator for the Environment Peter Strieder.
"It is at the point where we don't really know how we are going to finance the future," Strieder said in an interview with InfoRadio in Berlin.

Already over 50 billion marks in debt, Berlin has been forced to make draconian spending cuts. These have caused tensions to flare between the formerly communist eastern half of the city and the western half of Berlin, long pampered by generous subisides from Bonn during the Cold War years.
The debt is triple the level of West Berlin's indebtedness when the Berlin Wall was breeched in November 1989.
Despite the widely loathed spending cuts, Berlin's debt will still hit 76 billion marks in 1999 -- when the federal government is expected to move to Berlin.
Berlin will sell its 50.8 percent stake in BEWAG to German utility groups VIAG AG and Veba AG and U.S. utility Southern Co.
Berlin received a 45 million mark dividend payment from BEWAG last year.

Berlin is also planning to sell its 51 percent stake in the gas distribution company GASAG, for which it hopes to collect one billion marks. All together, Berlin is counting on asset sales bringing in nearly six billion marks this year.
"We will continue on this path soberly and coldly," said Annette Fugmann-Heesing, Berlin's Senator for Finance who has tried to slash spending and push asset sales through.
A member of the left-leaning Social Democrats (SPD), she admitted she has run into opposition from her coalition partners, the Christian Democrats.
"That crowd keeps fighting changes," she said.

With its finances in shambles, Berlin has been making painful cuts in local services. Kindergarten fees were recently raised sharply, entrance fees for swimming pools were doubled to eight marks, rubbish collection fees raised by 30 percent, and an annual "dog tax" nearly doubled to 300 marks. Lights are left off in some district buildings to save money.

Analysts at Berlin's DIW economic research institute say Berlin's problems were magnified after the Wall was brought down because there was two of everything -- city administrations, police forces, school systems and fire departments -- and the city has been slow to scale back.
At the same time, the federal government pulled out of the financing for Berlin, trimming its once-generous subsides to the capitalist enclave in the middle of communist East Germany.

Also harming Berlin was the fact that the industrial base in both east and west Berlin has been badly eroded as hundreds of companies have either folded or moved to sites outside the city where land and labour are far cheaper.
Berlin's unemployment rate is 15 percent, about four points above the national average. ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
